articles.title: Coral reefs are tougher than we thought
articles.excerpt: Coral reefs are small but mighty: covering less than 1% of the ocean floor, they support a quarter of all marine species. Up to 1 billion people also depend on reefs for food, storm protection – their structures reduce wave energy by up to 97% – and even medicine, with coral compounds used in treatments for cancer and arthritis. This year, we got good news about them: there are three times more coral reefs tough enough to survive a high-emissions climate crisis scenario for 2050 than a landmark 2018 effort found. Scientists from Macquarie University in Sydney and the Wildlife Conservation Society in New York looked at 165,922 km² worth of ocean floor across 71 countries, and found that reefs are more climate-resilient than we thought. articles.title: Can we refreeze the Arctic?
articles.excerpt: It's not news that we're losing Arctic ice fast: since the 1970s, Arctic summer sea ice volume has shrunk by at least 75%. What you may not know is how much our climate depends on it. Arctic ice reserves are the “refrigerator of the earth”, as Christian Haas puts it. He's a professor in geophysics at the University of Bremen and the head of the sea ice physics section at the Alfred Wegener Institute, and has studied sea ice for some 30 years. “When I started with my research, the ice was thicker than the size of a person.” Today, he said, that is no longer the case. A wider frozen surface is key to alleviating the effects of global heating. Ice reflects up to 85% of the sun’s heat back into space, while the open ocean reflects just 7%.
